title: 22. Interview: Durability
summary: Interview Q&A for Durability — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Durability interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between durability and availability? Give an example of each.
**Answer:** Durability is "once written, the data survives forever"; availability is "the system is up and serving requests right now." A system can be durable but unavailable: an offline backup tape in a vault is perfectly durable but the system cannot serve reads. A system can be available but not durable: an in-memory cache returns data instantly, but if the power fails, everything is lost. S3 is highly durable (11 nines) but during the 2017 us-east-1 outage it was unavailable for hours — data was safe, just unreachable. The distinction matters for design: durability requires redundancy and verification (replication + scrubbing), availability requires redundancy and failover (load balancers + health checks). The two are related — losing data typically also causes an outage — but the engineering mechanisms are different. A mature system tracks both as separate SLOs: "99.999999999% durability over a year" and "99.99% availability per month" are common split targets.
**Visual:**
```
                Durable?    Available?
Backup tape     yes         no (offline)
In-memory cache no          yes
S3 (normal)     yes         yes
S3 (2017 outage) yes        no (4h)
```

### Q2. Explain replication factor (RF) and quorum writes. Why does RF=3 with QUORUM give strong durability?
**Answer:** Replication factor RF is the number of replicas that store each piece of data — RF=3 means three independent copies. Quorum write W is the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write before the client is told "done." With RF=3 and W=2 (QUORUM), the write is acked after any two of three replicas persist it. This gives strong durability because the data survives the loss of any single replica — even if the third replica never received it, the two that did form a majority, and the system can still serve and recover the data. To lose the data, you would need to lose two replicas simultaneously before the third is repaired, which is astronomically unlikely with independent failure domains. The trade-off: W=2 means the write is only as fast as the second-fastest replica, slower than W=1 but more durable. W=ALL is the strongest but blocks on any unreachable replica; W=QUORUM is the practical sweet spot. Cassandra and Dynamo both default to this model.
**Visual:**
```
RF=3, W=2 (QUORUM):
  N1: ack  N2: ack  N3: slow
       \      /
        v    v
       ack client (2 >= W)
  Loses data only if N1 AND N2 fail before N3 catches up
```

### Q3. Compare replication vs erasure coding. When does each win?
**Answer:** Replication stores N identical copies; erasure coding splits data into k data chunks plus m parity chunks and stores k+m chunks across distinct failure domains, tolerating loss of any m. Replication wins on simplicity, read latency (any replica can serve a read), and write latency (one replica ack suffices). Erasure coding wins on storage efficiency — RF=3 costs 3x storage, while 10+4 erasure costs only 1.4x for the same fault tolerance (4 failures tolerated). The crossover: for cold storage where reads are rare and storage cost dominates (S3 Glacier, Azure Archive, GCP Archive), erasure coding is overwhelmingly favored — AWS S3 uses it internally. For hot storage where every replica serves reads (Cassandra, Redis Cluster, CockroachDB), replication wins because rebuilding an object from erasure chunks is expensive (read all k chunks, recompute parity) and adds latency. Hybrid systems use both: HDFS uses RF=3 for hot blocks and switches to erasure coding for cold files; Ceph uses replication by default but supports erasure-coded pools for cold storage.
**Visual:**
```
Replication RF=3:        Erasure 10+4:
  [A] [A] [A]            [d1][d2]...[d10][p1][p2][p3][p4]
  3x storage             1.4x storage
  tolerate 2 lost        tolerate 4 lost
  read from any          reconstruct from 10 of 14
```

### Q4. What is a silent data corruption, and how do storage systems defend against it?
**Answer:** Silent data corruption is when stored data is altered without any error signal — the disk returns bytes, but they are not the bytes that were written. Causes include bit rot on magnetic media, firmware bugs, controller errors, DRAM flips, and cosmic ray strikes on SSDs. The danger is that a backup that has been silently corrupted is worse than no backup — you trust it and discover the corruption years later when the original is gone. Storage systems defend with three layers: (1) Checksums on every block — S3 stores a checksum with every object and verifies it on every read; Cassandra computes checksums per SSTable and rejects mismatches. (2) Background scrubbing — a continuous process reads every stored object, recomputes its checksum, and repairs mismatches from replicas or parity. S3's scrubber is what makes their 11-nines durability real; without it, silent corruption would accumulate. (3) End-to-end checksums in the application — the client computes a checksum before upload and verifies after download, catching any corruption introduced anywhere in the path. The pitfall: checksums catch corruption but do not prevent it; you still need redundancy to repair.
**Visual:**
```
write:  data + checksum(data)  ->  disk
read :  data -> recompute checksum -> compare
                                     |
                            mismatch v
                              scrub/repair from replicas
```

### Q5. What is the durability window in async replication, and why does it matter?
**Answer:** The durability window is the gap between when a primary acknowledges a write to the client and when that write is replicated to the secondary. During this window, the data exists on only one node — if the primary crashes before replication completes, the write is lost even though the client was told it succeeded. This is the classic "data loss on failover" scenario. Async replication (Postgres streaming replication with default settings, MySQL binlog replication, Redis async replication) has a durability window of milliseconds to seconds; sync replication (Postgres synchronous_commit=on with sync replicas, CockroachDB, Spanner) has effectively zero durability window because the primary waits for the secondary to ack before acking the client, but it pays an extra round-trip of latency per write. The trade-off is fundamental: low-latency writes accept a small durability risk; zero-risk writes pay a latency tax. For a banking ledger, sync replication is mandatory; for a metrics pipeline, async with 100ms lag is fine. Knowing the durability window of your storage system is essential to setting correct client expectations.
**Visual:**
```
Async:  client --write--> primary --acks--> client
                          |
                          +-- replicate (async) --> secondary
                          ^ durability window here ^
        primary crashes here = DATA LOSS
```

### Q6. How does S3 achieve 11 nines of durability? Walk through the layered design.
**Answer:** S3's 11 nines come from layered defenses, not a single mechanism. (1) Within an AZ, objects are erasure-coded across many disks — a single disk failure does not lose data, and the system can reconstruct from parity. (2) Across AZs in a region, S3 replicates objects to three AZs by default, so an entire AZ failure (power, fire) does not lose data. (3) Cross-region replication (CRR) lets customers push objects to a second region for regional disaster recovery. (4) A continuous background scrubber reads every stored object, recomputes its checksum, and repairs any mismatches from replicas or parity — catching silent corruption before it accumulates. (5) Every read verifies the checksum before returning data to the client, catching any corruption introduced in the read path. The 11-nines number is a probabilistic calculation: with independent failures across AZs, the probability of losing all replicas of any single object in a year is below 10^-11. The system also publishes this as an SLA — if S3 ever does lose an object, AWS refunds a fraction of your S3 bill. The design is layered, not single-point: each layer covers a class of failure the others don't.
**Visual:**
```
[Object] -> erasure 10+4 (within AZ)
         -> replicate x3 AZs (within region)
         -> CRR to second region (cross-region)
         -> scrubber (continuous checksum verify)
         -> read-time checksum verify
```

### Q7. Why is "100% durability" not a real engineering target, and how do you choose the right level?
**Answer:** 100% durability is mathematically impossible at finite cost — every storage medium has a non-zero failure rate, and at scale, rare events become expected. Even S3's 11 nines means roughly 1 object lost per 10,000 years of storage — not zero. The practical question is: what is the cost of losing one object, and how much are you willing to pay to push the probability below your tolerance? Framework: (1) Estimate the business cost of losing an object (regulatory penalty, customer churn, lost revenue). (2) Estimate the cost of the next durability nine (more replicas, more parity, more scrubbing, more cross-region replication). (3) Stop where marginal cost exceeds marginal value. For a photo-sharing app, three nines (RF=2 in one region) is fine — losing a photo is annoying, not catastrophic. For a medical record, you need at least seven nines (multi-region RF=3 plus snapshots plus offsite backup). For a nuclear inspection log, you need air-gapped offline copies plus physical redundancy. Document the chosen durability level and the residual risk explicitly; "we chose RF=3 in one region, accepting 1-in-10^4 risk per year" is a defensible engineering decision, while "we have backups, we're fine" is not.
**Visual:**
```
Workload           Durability target    Mechanism
Photo album        3 nines (99.9%)      RF=2 single region
E-commerce cart    5 nines (99.999%)    RF=3 multi-AZ + snapshots
Banking ledger     7+ nines             RF=3 multi-region + WQL + WAL backup
Medical record     9+ nines             multi-region + offline tape + audit
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run a photo-sharing app storing 50PB of user photos. Storage costs are eating your budget. How do you reduce them without sacrificing durability?
**Answer:** The default setup is probably RF=3 in a single region, costing 150PB of physical storage. Three moves reduce cost without compromising durability. (1) Tier the storage: photos accessed in the last 30 days stay on hot storage (RF=3); older photos move to cold storage using erasure coding (e.g., 6+3, 1.5x overhead instead of 3x). This halves the cost of cold data with the same fault tolerance. (2) Use object lifecycle rules: after 90 days, move to standard-IA; after 1 year, move to Glacier-class storage (still 11 nines durable, but 1c/GB instead of 23c/GB). The trade-off is retrieval latency — Glacier retrieval takes minutes to hours, fine for archive photos but not for the main feed. (3) Deduplicate identical photos (multiple users posting the same meme) — content-addressable storage dedupes at the storage layer. The combination can cut storage costs by 70% with no durability loss. The pitfall: ensure the erasure coding and tiering configs are tested under recovery scenarios — being unable to reconstruct an object during an AZ failure is the kind of bug that doesn't surface until the worst moment.
**Visual:**
```
50PB logical
  hot (0-30d):  10PB * 3x   = 30PB  @ $23/TB  = $690/mo/TB logical
  warm (30-90d): 15PB * 3x  = 45PB  @ $12.5   = ...
  cold (90d+):   25PB * 1.5x = 37.5PB @ $4     = ...
Total ~112PB physical (vs 150PB at RF=3 everywhere)
```

### Q2. Your primary Postgres database crashes during a failover, and you discover 30 seconds of writes are missing from the replica. The CEO wants a post-mortem. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** The 30-second gap is the durability window of async replication: the primary accepted writes, acked them to clients, but had not yet shipped the WAL to the replica when it crashed. Those writes existed only in the primary's memory (or WAL not yet flushed), and the crash destroyed them. Prevention options, in order of cost: (1) Switch to synchronous replication with `synchronous_commit=on` and a synchronous standby — every write waits for the standby to ack, eliminating the durability window, at the cost of ~1 RTT per write (a few ms in-AZ, more cross-AZ). (2) Use synchronous replication only for the most critical tables (e.g., the payments table) and async for the rest — a hybrid that limits the latency penalty. (3) Reduce the WAL shipping interval from default to near-zero (already done in modern Postgres streaming replication, but check). (4) Add application-level idempotency so clients can safely retry — the lost writes will be re-issued and deduplicated. The post-mortem should explain that async replication has a documented durability window and the team either didn't know or accepted the risk; going forward, classify each table by durability need and configure replication accordingly. The CEO should understand that zero data loss requires sync replication, which costs latency.
**Visual:**
```
primary: W1 W2 W3 (acked, not yet shipped)
         |
       crash
         v
replica: W1 W2  (missing W3)
         ^
         | durability window = 30s
Fix: sync replication -> primary waits for replica ack before acking client
```

### Q3. You are designing storage for a banking ledger. The CTO says "we cannot ever lose a transaction." How do you respond?
**Answer:** Push back on the framing: "cannot ever lose" is not an engineering target — it is impossible at finite cost. Instead, propose a quantified durability target: "We will design for a probability of data loss below 10^-9 per year, with verified recovery drills quarterly." Concretely: (1) Multi-region active-active with synchronous replication (Spanner, CockroachDB, or Postgres with sync standbys in two regions) — every transaction is acked only after at least two regions have it. (2) Write-ahead log shipped to object storage (S3 with versioning) every few seconds as an additional immutable audit layer. (3) Daily full backups to a third region with offline copies — defends against software bugs that corrupt data across all live replicas. (4) End-to-end transaction checksums and periodic reconciliation against an independent ledger (e.g., a separate audit service that recomputes balances). (5) Quarterly disaster-recovery drills that simulate region loss and verify recovery time and data integrity. Document the residual risk explicitly: "We tolerate 1-in-10^9 chance of losing a transaction per year; the cost of pushing below that is X million dollars annually and adds Y ms of write latency." This is a defensible engineering position that the CTO can take to regulators.
**Visual:**
```
[Txn] -> primary (region A)
        -> sync replica (region B)  <-- both must ack
        -> WAL -> S3 (region C)     <-- immutable audit
        -> daily backup to region D
        -> quarterly DR drill verifies recovery
```

### Q4. Your Cassandra cluster shows read latency spikes every few hours. Investigation reveals read-repairs are pulling stale data from lagging replicas. What's the issue, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** Read-repair is Cassandra's mechanism for bringing lagging replicas up to date on reads: when a QUORUM read finds that replicas disagree, it writes the latest version back to all replicas. If write consistency is ONE (only one replica acked the original write) and reads are QUORUM, reads will frequently trigger read-repair because the other replicas are stale — and the repair adds latency to the read path. The fix has two angles. (1) Raise write consistency to LOCAL_QUORUM so writes are durable across multiple replicas before acking — this reduces the staleness gap that read-repair has to close. (2) Run nodetool repair regularly (every 5-7 days, or use incremental repair) so that anti-entropy happens in the background rather than on the read path. (3) Consider switching to read consistency ONE for low-staleness-tolerance workloads — this avoids the QUORUM read-repair cost but trades consistency. (4) Investigate the underlying cause of replica lag — typically compaction backlog or GC pauses — and fix that. The pitfall: simply disabling read-repair would hide the staleness but not fix it, and you'd eventually serve stale data. The right answer is to ensure replicas converge proactively rather than reactively on the read path.
**Visual:**
```
Write CL=ONE:   [N1 acks]  N2,N3 stale
Read CL=QUORUM: read N1,N2,N3 -> N2,N3 stale
                -> read-repair writes back to N2,N3
                -> extra latency on read path
Fix: write CL=LOCAL_QUORUM + scheduled nodetool repair
```

### Q5. You're designing a new object store for a startup. The team wants RF=3 for simplicity. Engineering wants erasure coding for cost. How do you decide?
**Answer:** The decision depends on workload characteristics and operational maturity, not on which is "better." Questions to ask: (1) What's the read/write ratio? Hot workloads with many reads favor replication (any replica serves reads); cold archival workloads favor erasure coding (storage cost dominates, reads are rare). (2) What's the storage scale? At 10TB, the 2x cost difference between RF=3 and 10+4 erasure is negligible — pick replication for simplicity. At 10PB, the difference is millions of dollars per year — erasure coding wins. (3) What's the team's operational maturity? Erasure coding adds reconstruction complexity, scrubbing, and chunk placement logic — a 5-person team will struggle; a 50-person storage team can handle it. (4) Are reads latency-sensitive? Erasure reconstruction adds latency to reads that hit degraded chunks. Recommendation for a startup: start with RF=3, abstract the storage layer so you can swap implementations later, and revisit erasure coding when storage costs cross 7 figures annually. The mistake to avoid: building erasure coding from day one and spending engineering resources that should go to product. Buy (use S3) until scale demands build.
**Visual:**
```
Scale       Read pattern     Maturity        Recommendation
< 100TB     hot              small team      RF=3 (or use S3)
100TB-1PB   mixed            medium          RF=3 + tier to S3-IA
> 1PB       cold-heavy       mature team     Erasure 10+4 or 6+3
> 10PB      mixed            mature team     Hybrid: hot RF=3, cold erasure
```

### Q6. A compliance team requires that deleted user data be "irrecoverably destroyed" within 30 days, but your storage system replicates to backups and snapshots. How do you reconcile this with durability?
**Answer:** This is the classic tension between durability (keep data forever) and the right to erasure (GDPR, CCPA). The naive approach — delete from primary storage — fails because backups and snapshots still contain the data. Reconciliation requires designing deletion as a first-class operation, not an afterthought. (1) Use object versioning with explicit delete markers; on deletion, mark deleted and propagate the marker to all versions, including backups. Restorations must apply the deletion marker. (2) For encryption-based destruction: encrypt each user's data with a per-user key, store the key in a separate KMS, and on deletion, destroy the key — the encrypted data becomes unrecoverable even if backups persist. This is called cryptographic erasure and is the industry standard for compliance. (3) Coordinate snapshot lifecycle so that snapshots older than the retention window are garbage-collected and the deletion marker is honored in restored snapshots. (4) Document the destruction timeline and audit trail — regulators want proof, not just a promise. (5) Test the deletion path: periodically delete a test user, restore backups, and verify the data is genuinely gone. The pitfall: treating deletion as a primary-only operation and forgetting snapshots — this is how companies fail GDPR audits and get fined.
**Visual:**
```
[user data] -> encrypt with per-user key
                |
            delete request -> destroy key in KMS
                          -> mark deleted in primary + all snapshots
                          -> snapshots older than 30d: GC'd
                          -> audit log records destruction
Even if backup restored, no key = unreadable ciphertext
```

### Q7. Your team's S3 bucket suddenly shows a 10x spike in 408 (timeout) errors. Objects are still there (no data loss) but reads are slow. What's happening, and how does durability relate to this?
**Answer:** The likely cause is a partial infrastructure issue — a disk or rack failing within an AZ, causing S3 to fall back to slower reconstruction paths or to other AZs. The objects are not lost (durability is intact — multiple replicas and parity exist), but reads that hit the degraded path are slower, causing client timeouts. This illustrates the durability-availability-latency triangle: high durability (multiple replicas) doesn't mean high availability or low latency — it just means the data survives. When S3 internally has to reconstruct an object from parity, the read takes much longer than serving from a healthy replica. Mitigations: (1) Implement client-side retries with exponential backoff and jitter — most transient S3 errors resolve on retry. (2) Use S3 Transfer Acceleration or CloudFront for latency-sensitive reads — the edge cache absorbs the spike. (3) Cross-region replicate critical objects so you can fail over to a healthy region if one region degrades. (4) Monitor S3's per-request latency, not just error rate — latency spikes precede error spikes and give you earlier warning. (5) If the issue persists, open an AWS support ticket — they will route around the degraded hardware internally. The lesson: durability and availability are separate SLOs; a system can be perfectly durable and still unusable if reads time out.
**Visual:**
```
[Client read] -> S3
                -> AZ-a: disk degraded, slow reconstruction
                -> AZ-b: healthy
                -> AZ-c: healthy
Client sees: 408 timeout (data still safe, just slow)
Fix: retry + backoff, or failover to AZ-b/c
```
